note.question: How should a retailer commit to disclose an early demand forecast so that its supplier produces more, and when does a tailored partial-disclosure policy outperform full or no disclosure?
note.overview: The retailer is an informed sender that commits ex ante to an information structure, and the supplier is a receiver that updates beliefs and chooses a newsvendor production quantity. The paper solves the sender-optimal Bayesian-persuasion outcome.

coverage.note: The existing independently audited model map was decomposed into Mini-style components and linked back to the page-preserving source extraction.

models.name: Retailer-designed demand disclosure to persuade a supplier's newsvendor production decision
models.summary: The retailer is an informed sender that commits ex ante to an information structure, and the supplier is a receiver that updates beliefs and chooses a newsvendor production quantity. The paper solves the sender-optimal Bayesian-persuasion outcome.
objects: A downstream retailer that observes a demand-state signal and designs disclosure
An upstream supplier that updates beliefs
inputs: Retailer and supplier share a common prior p_0 over the binary demand state
Both players know the two conditional demand distributions and the retailer's committed disclosure policy

assumptions: The baseline is a single-period, two-tier supply chain with one retailer, one supplier, and one product
The supplier incurs linear shortage and excess-inventory costs and chooses capacity before final demand is observed
The retailer observes final demand before ordering, so it bears shortage cost but no excess inventory in the baseline and always prefers a larger supplier quantity

models.method: The authors derive the supplier's posterior newsvendor quantile in closed form, express the retailer's expected shortage cost as a function of posterior beliefs, and use Bayesian-persuasion convexification to characterize optimal posterior splits.

sources.quote: The optimal policy characterization in Theorem 1 also enables us to shed light on how the critical ratio ξ and the retailer’s prior belief p0 affect the value of infor­ mation, which we define as the absolute value of the difference between the retailer’s expected cost under naive policies such as full and no disclosure and the optimal expected cost of the retailer.
